title: Vijayanagara empire: history, rulers and Hampi
seo_title: Vijayanagara Empire: Rulers, Administration and Hampi
meta_description: The Vijayanagara empire explained: its founding in 1336, four dynasties, Krishnadevaraya, the nayaka system, the Battle of Talikota and the ruins of Hampi.
summary: The Vijayanagara empire was founded around 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty and ruled much of south India until the 17th century. Its capital at Hampi on the Tungabhadra was one of the largest cities of its time. It peaked under Krishnadevaraya and was weakened after the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

paras: In the early 14th century the armies of the Delhi Sultanate raided deep into the Deccan and the south, overturning the Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and the kingdom of Kampili. In this unsettled time, two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, established a new kingdom on the Tungabhadra around 1336. Later tradition links them with the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri. The details of their early career, including whether they had served the Delhi sultan, are debated.

The capital, Vijayanagara (city of victory), was built around the much older sacred site of Hampi, associated with the Virupaksha temple and the goddess Pampa. Our guide to a [heritage walk in Hampi](heritage-walk-in-hampi.html) covers the site on foot.
Four dynasties ruled from Vijayanagara in turn. Each came to power after a usurpation, which shows how much depended on military commanders.

sections.h2: Krishnadevaraya and the height of the empire
paras: Krishnadevaraya (ruled 1509 to 1529) of the Tuluva dynasty is the best-known Vijayanagara ruler. He fought successfully against the Bahmani successor states and the Gajapatis of Odisha, and took the Raichur doab. He is also remembered as a patron of Telugu, Kannada, Sanskrit and Tamil literature and wrote the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada himself.

Portuguese visitors such as Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes, who came in the 1520s and 1530s, left descriptions of the city's markets, festivals and size. Paes compared it to Rome. Persian visitor Abdur Razzaq had described the city in the 1440s.

sections.h2: Administration: the nayaka and amara-nayaka system
paras: Vijayanagara rulers relied heavily on military chiefs called nayakas. Under the amara-nayaka system, a commander received the right to collect revenue from a territory (amaram) and in return maintained a fixed number of soldiers and horses and paid tribute to the king. Historians compare it with the Delhi Sultanate's iqta system.

The empire depended on cavalry, and imported horses from Arabia and Central Asia through west coast ports were a vital trade, first through Arab merchants and later through the Portuguese. Temples were major landholders and centres of local economy, and many inscriptions record grants to them. After the empire weakened, many nayakas, such as those of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee, became independent rulers.

sections.h2: The Battle of Talikota (1565) and after
paras: In January 1565 the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara near the villages of Rakkasagi and Tangadagi; the battle is commonly named after nearby Talikota. Aliya Rama Raya was killed and the capital was sacked and largely abandoned over the following months.

The empire did not end in 1565. Under the Aravidu dynasty it continued from Penukonda and then Chandragiri into the 17th century, though with far less power. Many nayaka families who had served the empire went on to build their own capitals and temples in the 17th century.

Vijayanagara's main rivals were the Bahmani sultanate, founded in 1347, and after about 1490 its five successor states: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar and Berar. Much of the conflict was over the fertile Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

Relations were not only hostile. Rulers on both sides hired soldiers from the other, shared courtly fashions in dress and architecture, and formed shifting alliances. Aliya Rama Raya, for example, intervened in the quarrels of the sultanates before they united against him. Buildings such as the Lotus Mahal at Hampi, with its cusped arches, show this shared Deccan style. Our guide to [heritage walks in Vijayapura (Bijapur)](heritage-walk-in-vijayapura.html) covers the other side of the frontier.

sections.h2: Vijayanagara architecture: what to see at Hampi
paras: Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1986. Its ruins divide roughly into a sacred centre along the river and a royal centre to the south. Vijayanagara temples are known for tall gateway towers (gopurams) built by the rulers, and pillared halls (mandapas) with rearing horse and yali brackets. The Vittala temple with its stone chariot and musical pillars, the Hazara Rama temple with its relief panels of royal processions, the Lotus Mahal and the elephant stables are highlights.

Our lecture on [Dravida temple architecture](dravida-temple-architecture.html) explains the temple forms, and the [south India temple architecture](south-india-temple-architecture.html) journey can include Hampi alongside Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal. For the wider region, see [heritage sites in Karnataka](heritage-sites-in-karnataka.html).

faq.a: The brothers Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty founded the Vijayanagara empire around 1336. Tradition links them with the sage Vidyaranya. Their kingdom grew to cover most of south India south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

faq.q: Who was the greatest ruler of Vijayanagara?
faq.a: Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty, who ruled from 1509 to 1529, is generally considered the greatest. He won major campaigns against the Deccan sultanates and the Gajapatis, built extensively at Hampi, and was a poet and patron of literature.

faq.q: Why did the Vijayanagara empire decline?
faq.a: Its defeat by an alliance of Deccan sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 and the sack of Hampi were decisive. Rivalries at court and the growing independence of the nayakas also weakened it. The Aravidu rulers continued from Penukonda and Chandragiri with reduced power.

faq.q: What was the capital of the Vijayanagara empire?
faq.a: The capital was the city of Vijayanagara, whose ruins are at Hampi in Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, on the south bank of the Tungabhadra. After 1565 the capital moved to Penukonda and later Chandragiri, both in present-day Andhra Pradesh.

faq.q: What are the main features of Vijayanagara architecture?
faq.a: Large gateway towers (rayagopurams), pillared halls with carved brackets of horses and yalis, temple chariot streets, stone chariots, and secular buildings such as the Lotus Mahal that combine Indian and Deccan sultanate features.

Visitors included the Italian Niccolò de' Conti in the early 15th century, the Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq in the 1440s, and the Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes in the 16th century. Their accounts describe the city's size, markets, festivals and court.

posts.hook: A Portuguese visitor compared Vijayanagara to Rome.
posts.caption: Domingo Paes, who saw the city in the 1520s, said it was as large as Rome and very beautiful. Today its ruins spread across the boulders of Hampi.

posts.hook: At the Hazara Rama temple, read the walls from bottom to top.
posts.caption: Bands of horses, elephants, dancers and soldiers show the Mahanavami festival processions. It is the closest thing to a film of court life in stone.
